title: Korea's lay founders (1784)
hook: Korean scholars read Christian books and founded their own church before any priest arrived

segments.voice: Yesterday, Japan's kakure kirishitan, keeping prayers by heart with no priests. Your line was hidden, but kept.

A handful of Korean scholars sit together over a pile of books. They're Confucian men, trained to read closely and argue carefully, and these books have come to them from Beijing, written in classical Chinese, the language of learning they all share. Some are about astronomy and mathematics. Some are about a Lord of Heaven. No missionary handed them over. No preacher is in the room. They're simply reading, and arguing, and reading again. What they did next is the story.

Among the books, the accounts say, was one written in Chinese by Matteo Ricci, the Jesuit from two days ago, about the Lord of Heaven. The scholars studied it the way they studied everything: closely. One of them, Yi Seung-hun, traveled to Beijing with a mission from the Korean court, found the Catholic church there, and asked to be baptized. He took the name Peter. When he came home, he baptized his friends. So a church began in Korea led entirely by laypeople, ordinary believers, not clergy. They met in homes, read together, and shared what they learned. For a while they even chose some of their own to lead worship as priests do, until they learned from the bishop in Beijing that only an ordained priest could do that, and they stopped. Acts describes some early believers who "received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily". These scholars did something like it, with no priest at their side. It cost them. The faith was soon outlawed, and persecutions came again and again. When a priest finally did arrive, he found a church already there. Catholics in Korea remember these founders and martyrs with honor. Look back at this whole week. Las Casas arguing against conquest. Mary at Guadalupe, in Catholic telling. Martin with his broom, Kateri in the woods, Ricci in scholar's robes, the hidden Christians in Japan. The faith met new peoples in very different ways. Here it arrived as a book, and readers did the rest.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've learned on this path that stayed with you: a line, a story, a person from this week. Say it to yourself in one plain sentence, the way you'd tell a friend at dinner. If you pray, pray for someone who might like to hear it; if you don't, just hold their name.
cheonju. Korean for the Lord of Heaven, the name for God that Korean scholars found in a book from Beijing and used to start a church led by laypeople.
Your line: the laity began it. Ordinary believers, reading together. Day nine hundred ten, done.

howItsDone: Catholics in Korea honor their founders and martyrs, visit shrines connected with them, and point to the church's lay beginnings as part of who they are.

chat.says: Who started the Catholic Church in Korea, if not missionaries?
options: Lay scholars who read books from Beijing and baptized their friends.
A Jesuit priest who sailed from China and preached at the court.
The Korean king, who had his whole court baptized in Beijing.
chat.meaning: Lay scholars read books from Beijing; Yi Seung-hun was baptized there and baptized his friends at home. When a priest arrived, a church was already there.

notes: Claims rule: no year or counts in the spoken text (the index title keeps 1784).

Ricci's Tianzhu shiyi among the books read in Korea; Yi Seung-hun baptized in Beijing as Peter; the lay community appointing its own 'priests' and stopping on the bishop's word; persecution; a priest (Zhou Wenmo) arriving later to find a church: confirm against Dallet and modern histories.
